content.overview: Git hooks are scripts that Git executes before or after events such as commit, push, and receive. They allow you to customize Git's behavior and automate tasks in your development workflow, from enforcing coding standards to triggering deployments.

steps.title: Understanding Git Hooks
steps.content: Git hooks are scripts that Git executes when certain events occur in your repository. They can be used to enforce standards, automate tasks, and integrate with other tools in your development workflow.

steps.title: Client-side Hooks
steps.content: Client-side hooks run on your local machine and can prevent commits or pushes that don't meet certain criteria. They're stored in the .git/hooks directory of your repository.

# it wants to stop the commit.
#

fileChanges.description: Create a pre-commit hook to run linters before committing
fileChanges.content:
#!/bin/sh

# Run linter on staged files
echo "Running linter..."
lint_output=$(npm run lint -- --staged)

# If linter found errors, prevent commit
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Linting failed. Please fix the errors before committing."
  echo "$lint_output"
  exit 1
fi

echo "Linting passed. Proceeding with commit."
exit 0

behindTheCommand.title: Common Client-side Hooks
behindTheCommand.content:
The most commonly used client-side hooks include:

1. **pre-commit**: Runs before a commit is created, often used for linting and testing
2. **prepare-commit-msg**: Runs before the commit message editor is launched
3. **commit-msg**: Validates the commit message format
4. **post-commit**: Runs after a commit is created, often used for notifications
5. **pre-push**: Runs before pushing commits to a remote repository

These hooks can prevent mistakes from entering your repository and enforce team standards.

steps.title: Creating a Custom Hook
steps.content: Creating a custom Git hook involves writing a script and making it executable. The script can be written in any language, but it must be executable by your system.

steps.title: Server-side Hooks
steps.content: Server-side hooks run on the remote repository when it receives pushed commits. They can enforce project policies and trigger integrations with other systems.

behindTheCommand.title: Common Server-side Hooks
behindTheCommand.content:
The most commonly used server-side hooks include:

1. **pre-receive**: Runs when the server receives a push, before any refs are updated
2. **update**: Runs once for each ref being updated
3. **post-receive**: Runs after all refs have been updated

Server-side hooks are powerful for enforcing organization-wide policies and triggering CI/CD pipelines.
